ch18.title: The Last Supper
ch18.b002: Thursday dawned clear. The spring sun came early over the camp on the slope of Olivet, and thin threads of cooking smoke rose between the tents. After breakfast the Master led the apostles and his closest disciples to a quiet spot a little above the camp. There were about fifty of them: men from Galilee, believers from Jerusalem, and the Greeks who had been staying in the camp. Peter counted the faces in the circle and found one missing.
ch18.b003: “I don’t see Judas,” he said to Andrew, who sat beside him.
ch18.b004: A few heads turned. Someone suggested the Master had sent him into the city on an errand; with the Passover so close, there must be a good deal to arrange. It sounded reasonable, and they all accepted it. There was nothing strange about the man who carried the bag going into the city on business. Only Andrew did not answer. He simply glanced once down the slope toward the city.
ch18.b005: The Master talked for almost two hours. He answered a score of questions about how the kingdom of heaven stood toward the kingdoms of this world, and about what kind of citizen a son of God ought to be in an earthly state. The kingdoms of this world, he said, might sometimes have to use force to keep order, but the kingdom of heaven could be spread only by the power of the spirit. They were to give Caesar what was Caesar’s and God what was God’s; only if some ruler presumed to take God’s place and demand their worship were they to worship God alone. Having become sons of the kingdom, they ought to be all the better citizens of the earthly one. And the gospel they would carry was like a living seed which, once planted, would keep unfolding in new forms from one generation to the next; they must never let it harden into a sacred memory, a mere tradition about him and his times.
ch18.b006: Simon Zelotes set his jaw every time the name of Caesar was spoken. Peter was snagged on something else. The Master was speaking of generations to come, of nations that would rise over long stretches of time. Yet for days now he had been saying again and again that he was about to leave them. A work that would reach down the ages, and an end that was coming soon — both were coming from the same mouth, and Peter could not fit them together. And the face of the speaker was strangely bright, almost carefree. That bright face and his own sense of a great disaster approaching would not match at all. That day it was the Greeks who understood him best.
ch18.b007: It was nearly one o’clock when they came down to the camp. David Zebedee and his helpers had lunch waiting. By then a rumor was going around the camp: Lazarus had fled from Bethany in haste. Peter stopped with a piece of bread half torn in his hands. Even the man who had been raised from the dead was being hunted. Now even a dull man could see what the rulers were after.
ch18.b008: The Man with the Water Pitcher
ch18.b009: After lunch John saw David lead the Master aside. David was his older brother, and his face was set hard. He seemed to begin a question and break off; John saw the Master lift a hand to stop him. John did not know what passed between them. David had men planted all over Jerusalem gathering news. What did his brother know? While John was turning that over, a runner arrived from Philadelphia, and the conversation between the two was cut short.
ch18.b010: Just then Philip came to the Master. The Passover was drawing near, he said; where would he have them make ready to eat it? It was a steward’s question. The Master told him to go and bring Peter and John: he would give them directions about the supper they would eat together that night, and as for the Passover, they could think about that afterward.
ch18.b011: Judas Iscariot was back in the camp. When he saw the Master talking with Philip he drifted quietly toward them. But David Zebedee, who was standing close by, stepped up and engaged him first: there were accounts to settle. Meanwhile Philip, Peter, and John drew off to one side with the Master.
ch18.b012: The Master told the three to go into Jerusalem at once. As they came in at the gate, a man carrying a water pitcher would speak to them, and they were to follow him. When he went into a certain house, they should ask the master of that house where the room was in which the Master would eat supper with his apostles. He would show them a large upper room, furnished and ready.
ch18.b013: On the way down to the gate John chewed over those directions. Why not simply tell them the place? Why follow a stranger with a pitcher? Near the gate, sure enough, a man with a water pitcher on his shoulder came up to them. Women usually carried the water jars, and that made him all the easier to notice. They followed him without a word through several turns of narrow lanes until they came to a gate. It was the house of John Mark. The boy’s father came out to meet them and showed them a broad room at the top of the stairs. Lamps hung there, couches were set out, and bread and wine were already on the table.
ch18.b014: Only then did John begin to understand a little. All this had been arranged beforehand. He remembered that the day before, the Master had spent the afternoon alone in the hills with John Mark. The Master wanted this last meal to be undisturbed by anyone. But John’s thoughts did not go so far as to ask who that anyone might be.
ch18.b015: At that same hour, back at the camp, Judas was sitting with David. As David took the money for provisions, he suggested gently that under the circumstances it might be wise to give him a little in advance of his actual needs. Judas thought for a moment. Then he said he would rather turn over all of it. Jerusalem was in such a state, and there were men plotting against the Master; if anything should happen to him, David’s work would not be held up.
ch18.b016: He counted out the apostolic funds and handed them to David, along with the receipts for all the money on deposit. His waist felt light. For more than three years that weight had hung on him like a part of his own body. Judas called it prudence — the proper thing for a far-seeing treasurer to do. He did not look closely at what he had just said, *if anything should happen to me*. He was not a man who looked long into his own heart. The other apostles did not learn of it until the evening of the next day.
ch18.b017: About half past four the three came back and reported that everything was ready. The Master set out at once with the twelve. It was the last road he would ever walk with all twelve of them.
ch18.b019: To avoid the people going back and forth in the Kidron valley, they crossed over the western brow of Olivet. When they came to the place where the Master had spoken the evening before about the fall of Jerusalem, they stopped without anyone deciding to. Below them the city lay in the slanting light. The white stone walls of the temple had turned gold, and over the countless roofs the evening smoke was beginning to rise. The Master did not want to pass through the city until after sunset, so they sat down there.
ch18.b020: He told them to rest, and began to talk. All these years, he said, he had lived among them as a brother and taught them the truth of the kingdom. They had been witnesses of the wonderful works of the Father and had shared in being fellow workers with God. He must go, but they must stay and finish the work he had begun; it was for this that he had set them apart in the hills near Capernaum.
ch18.b021: And when men came to take the Son of Man, he told them, they were not to throw themselves needlessly into danger. Just as he had sent Lazarus away so that he might live, they too must survive to be witnesses to the gospel. They should be valiant in defending the gospel by the power of the spirit, but they must not be drawn into any foolish attempt to defend the Son of Man. He needed no defense from human hands; the armies of heaven were already near.
ch18.b022: Peter’s hand went to his side before he knew it. When they left the camp that afternoon he had buckled on a sword. So had Simon Zelotes. No one had told them to. It was only that the city was said to be restless, and he had thought there ought to be at least one sword at the Master’s side. Now the Master was forbidding that very thought. Peter took his hand away. But he did not unbuckle the sword.
ch18.b023: In the Father’s universe, the Master went on, there were many dwelling places, and one day they too would rise to the worlds on high and sit with him. But first they must gird themselves and finish the work they had begun together, and before that they must pass through much tribulation and sorrow. Those trials, he said, were already upon them.
ch18.b024: When he had finished he stood up, and they all rose with him. They went down the darkening slope and into the city. The lanes before the Passover were jammed with pilgrims. Someone shouldered past them, a child was crying, somewhere a sheep bleated. No one recognized them. Of the twelve, only three knew where they were going. Judas Iscariot walked in the middle of the group. He watched the backs of Peter’s and John’s heads in front of him and wondered where they had gone that afternoon. Once they were through the gate, a boy who had been trailing them darted off down another lane and disappeared. John Mark meant to reach the house before them and be standing at the door.
ch18.b025: The Towel No One Took Up
ch18.b026: John Mark’s parents welcomed them warmly. The Master stayed downstairs to talk with the family, and the apostles went up first. The room was large and clean. A long table stood in the shape of a horseshoe, open at one end, and around it were thirteen couches for reclining at a meal. At one end of the table were bread, wine, water, and herbs — just such a table as a well-to-do Jewish household would set for the Passover. But there was no servant in sight. This evening belonged to the twelve alone.
ch18.b027: Just inside the door stood pitchers of water, basins, and towels, for washing the feet of guests who had come along dusty roads. When John Mark had gone back down, the apostles saw them, and then looked at one another. Who would wash their feet? No one asked it aloud. But each of them asked it inwardly, and each of them gave himself the same answer: not I. I am not the one who will play the servant in front of the others. The towels stayed where they hung beside the door.
ch18.b028: Still standing, they studied the seating. The host’s couch was a little higher. There was one place at its right, and the other eleven ran around the table to a point opposite that place on the right. Should they sit down, or wait for the Master to come and assign them their places? While they all hesitated, Judas Iscariot moved. He went to the seat of honor at the host’s left and made it plain that he meant to recline there as the preferred guest.
ch18.b029: The room erupted. Someone raised his voice. In the middle of the uproar John went to the place at the host’s right. Later John would ask himself why he had done it. He told himself it was only habit: at their common meals he usually sat at the Master’s right, and as one of his personal aides he was used to being at his side. But he knew it was not habit alone that had moved his feet. The moment he saw Judas take the left, a thought had moved his body before he could think it — that he would not let the right be taken too. It was the old pride of the youngest — the youngest son of his father’s house and the youngest of the twelve.
ch18.b030: Peter went red in the face. Judas on the left, John on the right. He was too angry to speak. With the others glaring, he marched all the way around the table and threw himself down on the last couch, directly opposite John — the lowest place of all. It was a protest. But it was not only a protest. In a corner of Peter’s heart there was another calculation. When the Master came in and saw him at the very bottom, surely he would call him up higher, and whoever had dared to take a high seat would be sent down. That was how Peter remembered the Master’s story about taking the lowest place at a feast.
ch18.b031: The rest took their places, some near Judas, some near Peter. At the Master’s right, John; at his left, Judas, then Simon Zelotes, Matthew, James Zebedee, Andrew, the Alpheus twins, Philip, Nathaniel, Thomas, and at the very end Simon Peter. They had come together to remember the night their fathers came out of slavery in Egypt. It was their last table with the Master. And there, once again, they were quarreling over who was greatest.
ch18.b032: Sharp words were still flying when the Master appeared in the doorway. He stopped on the threshold for a moment. As he looked around the room, a look of disappointment spread slowly over his face. John saw it, and could not breathe. The Master said nothing. He walked to his place and lay down, and he did not change a single one of their seats. Their feet were still unwashed. Their hearts were less washed still.
ch18.b034: For a while no one spoke. The Master looked around at each of them and then smiled, a smile meant to loosen the tight air. He told them how greatly he had longed to eat this meal with them before he suffered. What happened tomorrow was in the Father’s hands, he said; he would not eat with them like this again until they sat down together in the kingdom.
ch18.b035: The wine was mixed with water and the cup was brought to him; it came from the hand of Thaddeus, one of the twins. The Master gave thanks and told them to divide the cup among themselves. This was their last supper, he said; he would not drink the fruit of the vine with them again.
ch18.b036: He knew. He knew that his hour had come, and that Judas Iscariot had made up his mind to betray him that very night. Yet only one concern weighed on him: what would become of these men he had chosen.
ch18.b037: When they had drunk the first cup, the Master rose. By Jewish custom the host got up after the first cup to wash his hands. But the apostles knew he did not keep that rite, and so, when he walked quietly toward the door, they all watched him with curiosity. He took off his outer garment. He tied a towel around his waist. Then he tipped a pitcher and began to pour water into a basin. The sound of water falling into the basin filled the room. Curiosity turned to astonishment.
ch18.b038: The Master carried the basin around the open end of the table. He stopped at the lowest place, in front of Simon Peter, and knelt down as a servant kneels.
ch18.b039: At that, all twelve sprang to their feet as one man. Even Judas Iscariot stood. For that one moment even he forgot what he was carrying in his heart.
ch18.b040: Peter stood looking down. The face of his kneeling Master was turned up toward him. The Master said nothing. There was no need for words; his posture said everything. Something in Peter turned over. Who was this? On the hill near Caesarea-Philippi Peter had cried out that this was the Deliverer, the Son of the living God. Of all the twelve, he had been the first to say it aloud, and he had never since doubted it. And now this one was kneeling like a slave in front of his dusty feet. His soul could not bear it.
ch18.b041: At last he found words. Did the Master really mean to wash his feet? The Master looked up at him and said that he might not understand it now, but later he would know what it all meant. Peter drew a long breath. Then he said flatly that the Master would never wash his feet. The other apostles nodded. Peter had spoken for them all.
ch18.b042: Judas Iscariot too was shaken by the scene, at least for the first instant. But soon his mind began to sit in judgment on it. The man who was to save Israel, kneeling like a servant with a basin! Here was one more proof. This man would never mount a throne. And so the decision Judas had made was not a mistake. He reached that verdict, and when he had reached it his heart went cold again.
ch18.b043: The Master told Peter that unless he washed his feet, Peter would have no part with him in what he was about to do. Peter heard, and saw the Master still kneeling at his feet. He did not understand. But slowly he began to feel that something here touched on whatever would bind him to the Master in the time to come. And at once he swung to the other extreme. Then, he cried, not his feet only, but his hands and his head too! Peter was always like that. He leapt from one end to the other in a single bound.
ch18.b044: The Master said that one who had already bathed needed only his feet washed. They who sat with him tonight were clean — but not all of them. The dust on their feet ought to have been washed away before they sat down to eat, he said; he was doing this as a parable, to show them the meaning of a new commandment he was about to give them.
ch18.b045: Cold water touched the top of Peter’s foot. He flinched. The Master’s hands closed around his foot — a carpenter’s hands, thick-knuckled and hard. Peter knew those hands. Three years before, in the highlands, they had rested on his head. Now they were washing the dust from between his toes. Tears blurred Peter’s sight until he could not look down any longer.
ch18.b046: In silence the Master went around the table, washing their feet one by one. Thomas, Nathaniel, Philip, the twins. Andrew, James, Matthew, Simon Zelotes. And Judas Iscariot.
ch18.b047: Judas sat on the edge of his couch and put out his feet. The Master’s hands lifted them. The dust of the roads Judas had walked alone that morning loosened into the water of the basin. Judas looked down at the crown of the Master’s head. The hands did not hurry. They were as careful as they had been with Peter’s feet, and they lingered just as long; not a moment shorter. Judas could hardly bear it. If only he had been handled roughly. If only he had been passed over. Then he would have had one more reason to hate these hands. The towel dried the water from his feet. Only then did Judas realize he had been holding his breath.
ch18.b048: Last of all the Master washed John’s feet, then put his cloak back on and returned to his place. He looked at their bewildered faces and asked whether they understood what he had done to them. They called him Master, and they were right to. But if their Master had washed their feet, why had they been unwilling to wash one another’s? A servant was not greater than his master, nor one who was sent greater than the one who sent him. And when they came into this room, he said, they had not only refused to wash one another’s feet; they had fallen to quarreling over the places of honor. Did they not yet know there could be no place of preference at his table — that he loved each one of them just as he loved the others? The kings of the gentiles lorded it over their people, but among them it must not be so. Whoever would be great must become like the younger, and whoever would be first like one who serves. Which was greater, the one who sat at the table or the one who served? And he told them that he was among them as one who serves.
ch18.b049: John could not lift his head. He was lying at the Master’s right hand. That place had never felt so heavy. At the far end, opposite him, Peter too sat with his head bowed. The one who had seized the high place and the one who had waited at the bottom to be called up were equally ashamed.
ch18.b050: When the Master had finished, the twins got up and brought in the next course: bread and wine, bitter herbs, and a paste of crushed dried fruit. As always, they carried the dishes without a word. Tonight everyone noticed them. From the very beginning they had been the ones who served.
ch18.b052: For the first few minutes they ate in silence. But drawn by the Master’s cheerful face they began, little by little, to talk, and before long the meal was moving along warmly, as though nothing had happened. Nathaniel said something, and a few of them laughed. John found it a marvel. The shame of a few minutes ago was not gone, but something warm had been laid over it.
ch18.b053: When the second course was half finished, the Master looked around at them and spoke. Knowing that the forces of darkness were plotting the death of the Son of Man, he said, he had decided to eat this supper with them in this hidden room, a day ahead of the Passover. By this time tomorrow night he would not be with them. The hour had come for him to return to the Father. And then he added: but it had not been required that one of them should hand him over to his enemies.
ch18.b054: The table froze. Already stripped of much of their self-assurance by the foot washing and the words that followed it, they looked at one another. And one by one, stumbling, they asked: Is it I? Peter asked it, and Andrew asked it, and the twins asked it almost in the same voice. No one pointed at anyone else. Each laid a hand on his own breast.
ch18.b055: The Master said that his going to the Father was necessary, but it had not been necessary for one of them to become a traitor in order to accomplish it. This was the fruit of evil hidden in the heart of one who had failed to love the truth with his whole soul. And he lamented how deceitful was the pride of the intellect that comes before spiritual downfall. A friend of many years, one who was even now eating his bread, was willing to betray him; he was even now dipping his hand with him in the dish.
ch18.b056: They began to ask again: Is it I? And Judas Iscariot, reclining at the Master’s left, asked it too. Is it I?
ch18.b057: Judas heard his own voice. It had the same pitch, the same tremor as the others. A good imitation, he thought. At that moment the Master dipped a piece of bread in the dish of herbs and handed it to him. And quietly he said: You have said it.
ch18.b058: The bread was warm and moist. Judas sat holding it and could not move. The others had not heard. It was an ordinary courtesy for the host to hand a dipped morsel to the guest on his left, and no one paid it any heed. But Judas knew. He knew to the marrow what the gesture and the words meant. Suddenly he was afraid. What if the others had now guessed it too? He put the bread in his mouth. He could not chew.
ch18.b059: At the Master’s right John leaned toward him. Who was it, he whispered; they ought to know who had been false to his trust. The Master said he had already told him: it was the one to whom he had given the dipped bread. John raised his head and looked. He had seen the bread pass from the Master’s hand to the left. But to him it looked like nothing more than a host’s courtesy. The answer had been right before his eyes, and he had not seen it.
ch18.b060: At the far end of the table Peter leaned far forward.
ch18.b061: “John, ask him who it is. Or if he’s told you, tell me.”
ch18.b062: John shook his head. He did not know either. Whispers ran down the table. The Master put an end to them. He grieved, he said, that this evil had come about; until this very hour he had hoped that the power of truth would triumph over the deceptions of evil. But such victories were not won without the faith that comes from sincerely loving the truth. He would rather not have spoken of these things at their last supper, but he was telling them beforehand so that they would be ready for what was now upon them. After he was gone, they should remember that he had known of all this and had warned them — and he told them so that they might be strong in the trials ahead.
ch18.b063: Then the Master leaned toward Judas, and told him to do quickly what he had decided to do.
ch18.b064: Judas stood up. His couch scraped on the floor. He crossed the room without looking at anyone. The basin was still standing by the door. He stepped around it and opened the door. Below, the stairs were dark. He went out into the night.
ch18.b065: In those few steps a tangle of voices filled his head. He had been found out. No — found out only by the Master. And the Master had not rebuked him. He had sent him away. He had told him to be quick. Was that permission, or a test? Very faintly he heard a voice saying that it was not yet too late. But he laid another thought over it. Perhaps the man would show his power at the last moment. Perhaps only when he was cornered would he finally use it. Then what Judas had done would not be betrayal at all, but a push in the right direction. He raised that thought like a shield. The cold air of the lane touched his face. He quickened his pace.
ch18.b066: The men in the room saw Judas go and thought nothing of it. He had gone to buy something more for the supper, they supposed, or, since he carried the bag, the Master had sent him on some errand. There was no one in that room who knew the bag was no longer at his waist.
ch18.b067: The Master knew now that nothing could keep Judas from turning traitor. He had begun with twelve; now there were eleven. Judas was not one of those the Master had chosen himself. He had been brought in by the first apostles. Yet the Master had accepted him, and up to this very hour he had done everything possible to cleanse and save him, as he had for all the others. This evening, filled with tender moments and softening touches, had been his last call to the man who was leaving. But when love has once died in a heart, even the gentlest warning only hardens its hatred.
ch18.b069: The third cup was brought to the Master — the one called the cup of blessing. He rose from his couch, took it in both hands, and blessed it. They were all to drink of it, he said. This would be the cup of his remembrance, the cup of a new age of grace and truth, the emblem of the Spirit of Truth who would come to them and dwell with them. He would not drink this cup with them again until he drank it with them in a new form in the Father’s eternal kingdom.
ch18.b070: The cup went around the table and came to John. He took it in both hands. Lamplight trembled on the red wine. He remembered how, a little earlier, he had moved first to claim this place. With those same hands he was now receiving this cup. John drank, and passed it to the man beside him. No one spoke. They all sensed that something out of the ordinary was happening in that room. The old Passover remembered the night their fathers had gone free from slavery. But tonight the Master was asking them to remember something else. They did not fully know what it was. But the silence belonged to all of them.
ch18.b071: When the cup had come back, the Master took the bread, gave thanks, broke it, and told them to pass it around. He had told them, he said, that he was the bread of life; the word of the Father, revealed in the Son, was itself the bread of life. The pieces passed from hand to hand. There was the small dry sound of bread breaking. They ate, and sat down.
ch18.b072: For a moment no one moved. Then the Master spoke again. Whenever they did this, they were to remember the life he had lived among them, and to rejoice that he would go on living and serving on earth through them. They were not to contend over who was greatest, but to be as brothers; and when the kingdom had grown into great companies of believers, those companies too must not strive for greatness over one another.
ch18.b073: It was the upper room of a friend’s house. There was no priest, no consecrated altar, no fixed form of prayer. The Master did not pin down in words what he meant that evening. He only suggested it, by symbols. He wanted its meaning not to be shut up later in a rigid formula, but to stay alive and moving in each heart.
ch18.b074: The Master said to the eleven that whenever they did this, they should do it remembering him: first looking back on the days he had lived with them in the flesh, then looking forward in faith to the day when they would eat with him again in the Father’s kingdom. This, he told them, was the new Passover he was leaving with them — the memory of his life, the word of eternal truth, his love for them, and the Spirit of Truth soon to be poured out on all flesh.
ch18.b075: John looked around the table. At the Master’s left one couch was empty. The cushion still bore the dent where someone had leaned. John looked at it a long time. But even now he did not grasp what that empty place was telling him.
ch18.b076: Together they sang the one hundred and eighteenth Psalm. So ended a Passover without a slain lamb. Peter’s deep voice, from the lowest place, rang out the loudest.
ch18.b078: When the singing ended, they all supposed they would now go back to the camp. But the Master told them to stay seated. They remembered, he said, how he had once sent them out without purse or bag, and they had lacked nothing. But now hard times had come, and they could no longer count on the goodwill of the crowds. Whoever had a purse should take it; when they went out to preach the gospel, they should make what provision seemed wise for their own support. He had come to bring peace, but that peace would not appear for a while. Now the hour had come for the Son of Man to be glorified. He would be with them only a little longer, and he was going where they could not come.
ch18.b079: After some free talk the Master stood again. When he had shown them how to serve one another, he said, he had promised them a new commandment; now that he was leaving, he would give it. They knew well the commandment to love their neighbor as themselves, but he was not wholly satisfied with that. They were to love one another as he had loved them. By that, everyone would know they were his disciples.
ch18.b080: It was not a new burden, he said, but a new joy. No one has greater love than this, that he lays down his life for his friends — and they were his friends. They had called him Master, but he did not call them servants. They had not only chosen him; he had chosen them.
ch18.b081: Peter’s throat tightened at that. Friends. The man who had sat at the bottom of the table waiting to be called up — the Master had called him friend. Lay down his life for his friends, Peter thought. That much he could do. No, he would do it now, this very night. He felt again the hilt of the sword at his side. That was how he heard the words.
ch18.b082: The Master rose again and told them he was the true vine, the Father was the husbandman, and they were the branches. A branch bears fruit only while it stays on the vine; if they abode in him and his words lived in them, they would bear much fruit. As the Father had loved him, so he had loved them; they were to remain in his love. As they listened, every one of them thought of the same thing: the great carving of a vine and its clusters that adorned the entrance to Herod’s temple, a memorial of the old teaching that the Messiah would spring from the vine of David. They had walked beneath it every day, and never once had it occurred to them that it could mean this.
ch18.b083: The talk about the vine buzzed on for some time. When it had barely died down, the Master told them not to lose heart if the world hated them. It had hated him first. A servant was not greater than his master; those who had persecuted him would persecute them. But he would not leave them alone in the world; soon after he was gone he would send them a spirit helper. They were not to let their hearts be troubled. They believed in God; let them go on believing in him as well. In the Father’s universe there were many dwelling places, and he would go ahead and send for them.
ch18.b084: When the Master sat down, Thomas stood up. They did not know where the Master was going, he said, so how could they know the way? But if only he would show them the way, they would follow him this very night. It was so like Thomas: the doubting question and the vow to follow came out in a single breath. The Master told Thomas that he himself was the way, the truth, and the life. No one came to the Father except through him; if they knew him, they knew the way to the Father. And they did know him, for they had lived with him, and they were looking at him now.
ch18.b085: That was too deep for many of them, and especially for Philip. After a few words with Nathaniel beside him, Philip stood up. If only the Master would show them the Father, he said, everything he had told them would become plain.
ch18.b086: Several of them held their breath. It was always so with Philip. In the middle of the deepest words he asked for something he could hold in his hands. *Show us.* That was the way the world made sense to Philip. The Master did not rebuke him. He only looked at him for a long time and asked whether, after so long together, Philip still did not know him. Whoever had seen him had seen the Father; how then could Philip ask to be shown the Father? Let him believe that he was in the Father and the Father in him — or, if that was hard, let him believe for the sake of the life he had seen him live.
ch18.b087: Philip sat down slowly. For more than three years he had looked at that face every day. The hands that had handed out the barley loaves, the feet that had gathered the dust of the roads, the face that smiled on weary evenings. To have seen that, the Master said, was to have seen the Father. Philip did not understand all of it. But he did have the feeling that something had been in front of his eyes all along while he was looking somewhere else.
ch18.b088: When the Master stepped aside for a drink of water, the eleven burst into talk. Peter jumped up as if he had been waiting for the chance and began what was plainly going to be a long speech. Just as he drew breath, the Master came back and motioned them all to sit down. Peter shut his mouth and sat. Nathaniel turned his head to hide a smile.
ch18.b089: After he had gone to the Father, the Master told them, he would pour out the Spirit of Truth upon all flesh. He would not leave them desolate. Now he could be beside them only in his body; then he would be with each of them wherever they were. In a few hours the world would see him no more, but they would go on knowing him in their hearts.
ch18.b090: While the Master paused, Judas Alpheus spoke up. The twins hardly ever asked a question in front of the others. The Master had always lived among them as a friend, he said; if from now on he showed himself only by this spirit, how would they know him? If the world could not see him, how would they be sure? The Master looked down on them all and smiled. My little children, he called them. Soon they would not see him in flesh and blood, but he would send them his spirit, just like himself except for this material body. That new teacher would live in each of their hearts.
ch18.b091: Judas Alpheus did not understand all of it. But he did grasp that a new teacher was coming. He turned and looked at Andrew’s face. Andrew was quietly nodding. That was enough. Judas Alpheus glanced at his brother James, and the two of them were reassured at almost the same instant.
ch18.b092: Peter, James, John, and Matthew asked the Master several more questions. He warned them that they would be put out of the synagogues, and that the time was coming when those who killed them would think they were doing God a service. It was for their good that he was going away, he said; unless he went, the new teacher could not come. He had much more to tell them, but they could not bear it now. In a little while they would not see him; and in a little while after that they would see him again, but not for long, because he would be on his way to the Father.
ch18.b093: They murmured among themselves. What did he mean by “a little while”? And what did he mean, “not for long”? The Master knew what they were asking and told them plainly: the Son of Man must die, but he would rise again. As a woman in labor forgets her pain once her child is born, so their sorrow would be turned into joy.
ch18.b094: They looked at one another and said that now at last he was speaking plainly; surely he had come from God. And yet they still could not understand why he must go back to the Father. A glorious kingdom raised on earth by the son of David — they had carried that picture too long. The more firmly they believed him to be the Messiah, the more firmly that picture set within them, until it stopped their ears.
ch18.b095: The lamp oil had burned low and the flames had sunk. Outside the window it was deep night. Andrew saw his brother Peter sitting with his fists clenched on his knees. It was the face of a man who had made up his mind about something. And Andrew’s eyes went back once more to the empty couch at the Master’s left. Judas had not returned. The others supposed his errand was taking a long time. Andrew could not suppose so. He remembered a hand plucking at blades of grass in the highlands three years before. But he said nothing of it to anyone. Speaking of what he was not sure of was not his way. Whether that way had been right, the Andrew of that night did not ask.
ch18.b097: The events follow Papers 178–180: the Thursday forenoon discourse and the absence of Judas (178:0.1–2.1); the flight of Lazarus from Bethany (178:2.2); David Zebedee’s attempted question and the messenger from Philadelphia (178:2.3–2.4); Philip’s question, the man with the water pitcher, and the home of John Mark (178:2.5–2.9); Judas turning over all the apostolic funds to David (178:2.10–2.11); the talk on the brow of Olivet and the entry into the city after sunset (178:2.12–3.6); the furnishing of the upper room, the basins for washing feet, the dispute over seats, and the seating order (179:0.4–1.8); the first cup and the washing of feet (179:2.1–3.10); the foretelling of the betrayal, the dipped bread, and Judas’s departure (179:4.1–4.8); the cup of blessing, the bread of remembrance, and the one hundred and eighteenth Psalm (179:5.1–5.10); and the farewell discourse — the new commandment, the vine and the branches, and the questions of Thomas, Philip, and Judas Alpheus (180:0.1–6.9). That Peter and Simon Zelotes left camp that afternoon wearing swords comes from 183:2.2.
ch18.b098: Character details come from Paper 139 and related passages: Peter as the first to confess the Master’s divinity, and his swings from one extreme to the other (139:2, 179:3.2, 179:3.5); John as the youngest of his family and of the twelve, one of Jesus’ personal aides, and his usually well-concealed conceit, and his usual place at the Master’s right at meals (139:4.3–4.5, 139:4.10); Philip’s “show us” (139:5); the twins seldom asking questions in public (180:4.4); Andrew’s early awareness of Judas’s trouble, which he kept to himself (139:1.8); and Judas’s notion that Jesus might use his power at the last moment (139:12.12).
ch18.b099: Added fiction includes the apostles’ inner thoughts and feelings; the weather and the streets of the city; the short exchanges between Peter and John; John watching his brother David’s face; the sensations and gestures as the feet were washed and the cup and bread passed; and small moments such as Nathaniel hiding his smile when Peter’s speech was cut short. Where Judas went that morning is not stated in the text, so it is not told here.
ch18.b100: The words of Jesus are retold, not quoted, following the sense of the text.
